books.section: Topic 4.5 The Market Revolution: Economic Transformations

stimulus.source_note: View on the Erie Canal, published 1832 (New York Public Library); public domain.
stimulus.text: An 1832 view of the Erie Canal at night: a canal boat carrying passengers glides along the water under a full moon, with trees lining both banks and a bridge ahead.

figures.caption: View on the Erie Canal, 1832
figures.alt: An 1832 night view of the Erie Canal, a passenger boat gliding on moonlit water between tree-lined banks

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, View on the Erie Canal (1832), public domain
stem: The boat in the image is carrying passengers and goods along a canal. What was the main purpose of canals like this one in the 1820s and 1830s?

options.text: To carry farm goods and manufactures cheaply between West and East.
To carry enslaved people from the South to northern factories.
options.misconception: Canals carried freight and passengers, not enslaved people to factory jobs; the slave trade moved south and west.

options.text: To supply drinking water to the people of New York City.
options.misconception: The canal was a shipping route, not a water supply; New York's drinking water came from elsewhere.

options.text: To defend the Great Lakes against British warships.
options.misconception: The canal was built for trade, not defense; no warships used it to guard the lakes.

rationales.A: The canal was a shipping road. It moved western grain east and eastern factory goods west, cheaply and in bulk.
rationales.B: Canals carried freight and passengers, not enslaved people to factory jobs. The domestic slave trade moved south and west.
rationales.C: The canal was a shipping route, not a water supply. New York's drinking water came from elsewhere.
rationales.D: The canal was built for trade, not defense. No warships used it to guard the Great Lakes.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the boat. It is a cargo and passenger boat, not a warship or a water pipe.
2. Ask what it carries. Grain, lumber, cloth, and people, moving between farms and ports.
3. Ask why water beats wagons. A boat carries far more, far cheaper, than a wagon on a muddy road.
4. Put it together. Canals existed to move things cheaply, and that cheap movement built the national market.
Remember: in the 1820s, a canal was a highway for goods, and cheap goods travel far.
